 Red Hook Eminent Domain Determination Upheld as Appellate Court Rejects Boat Club Challenge 
 Open Audio Article Player 
 By aleah@thedailycatch.org 
 on 
 October 22, 2026 
 By Aleah Gatto & Emily Sachar 
 The Town of Red Hook won a major legal victory Wednesday in its effort to acquire the Red Hook Boat Club through eminent domain, as a state appellate court unanimously upheld the Town Board’s determination to take the club’s Hudson River property for a public waterfront park.
 A state appellate court unanimously upheld the Red Hook Town Board’s determination to acquire the Red Hook Boat Club. (Photo by Tony Adamis) 
 The Appellate Division, Second Department, rejected the club’s challenge to the acquisition, finding that the Town had established a legitimate public purpose, complied with environmental review requirements and adequately explained why its proposal was consistent with local waterfront policies.
 The Oct. 21 ruling upholds the Town Board’s July 15, 2025, resolution to acquire the land. It represents a substantial setback for the club’s effort to retain its property, although the judgment does not itself transfer ownership to the Town or determine the price of the acquisition.
 “Developing parkland and recreational space, as well as maintaining open space, are legitimate public uses,” the court wrote. “The [boat club] identified no ground for annulling the [Town] Board’s determination to proceed with acquiring the property by eminent domain.”
 The Town, the judges wrote, also need not find other land to create the public park it desires. “The Board has broad discretion to decide which land is necessary to fulfill its stated purpose,” the decision states.
 Richie Ross, Commodore of the Boat Club, said the organization was frustrated by the ruling. “We are even more disappointed that a town can wield the extraordinary power of eminent domain without a site plan or proper environmental review,” he told The Daily Catch Thursday. “At a time of heightened political turmoil, actions like this only further divide a small community.”
 Ross said that club members will continue to explore all legal options to thwart the Town’s plans, though he did not indicate on Thursday what those may be. Ross has also said previously that the club would work vigorously to defeat Town Supervisor Robert McKeon, Deputy Supervisor Bill Hamel, and Town Board member Jacob Testa, who have consistently supported the eminent domain action.
 McKeon told The Daily Catch Thursday that he is pleased with the ruling. “The Court’s unanimous decision confirms the Town did its due diligence in determining that this is the only viable property,” he said. “We look forward to moving ahead with a Town waterfront park.”
 The dispute has prompted significant public opposition, including a public meeting attended by over 500 people, nearly 100 of whom spoke against the proposal. (Photo by Athan Yanos) 
 In July 2025, the Town Board formally authorized the taking of two adjoining waterfront parcels totaling approximately 2.37 acres, including the property at 256 Dock Road. The Boat Club has challenged the Town’s actions through multiple lawsuits, one of which found deficiencies in the Town’s compliance with state environmental review requirements.
 The dispute has also prompted significant public opposition, including a 2025 public meeting attended by over 500 people, nearly 100 of whom spoke against the proposal, with concerns ranging from the use of eminent domain to the project’s cost, environmental review, and feasibility.
 McKeon said the Town will now move to purchase the property from the club, an action that must be completed within three years, according to the state’s eminent domain law. McKeon told The Daily Catch that the clock starts now, following the court’s decision Wednesday.
 The Town, McKeon said, cannot comment on its negotiations to purchase the land. The two parcels owned by the Red Hook Boat Club are currently assessed at a combined market value of about $1.3 million, according to Dutchess County Parcel Access, a property database.
 Kristina Dousharm, a member of the Red Hook Town Board who has been vocal in her opposition to the Town’s attempts to acquire the land, said that the Appellate Court decision was unfortunate, although somewhat expected. 
 Dousharm, along with Board Member Ken Migliorelli, have been the two dissenting votes in the purchase plan since their election to the board in November 2025. In July, Dousharm made a motion to hold a public referendum on the Town’s effort to take over the land, which was shot down by McKeon, Hamel, and Testa.
 “There are many things that are unclear,” said Dousharm, noting that the Town has not planned an allocation of money to purchase, build up, or maintain the property, nor has it addressed specific questions about how the land will be used.
 The appellate court’s decision follows arguments heard Oct. 5 before Justices Lara J. Genovesi, Valerie Brathwaite Nelson, Lillian Wan, and Laurence L. Love. All four concurred. The Appellate Division is the legal body in New York State that rules on the viability of all eminent domain actions.
 Commodore Richie Ross said that club members will continue to explore all legal options to thwart the Town’s plans, though he did not indicate on Thursday what those may be. (File photo) 
 The club brought its challenge under Section 207 of New York’s Eminent Domain Procedure Law, which provides for judicial review of a government’s determination to acquire property. The court emphasized that its review was limited, including whether the Town followed required procedures and whether the acquisition would serve as a public benefit.
 On that central question, the judges found that the club had failed to prove that the Town’s decision was irrational. In other words, they found the Town had a plausible public-interest reason for pursuing the property.
 The Town properly identified the proposed public use, explained its choice of location, and considered alternatives that it found inferior, the court concluded. The club’s contention that other locations would better serve the Town’s waterfront recreation goals did not provide a basis to overturn the determination.
 “The Board has broad discretion to decide which land is necessary to fulfill its stated purpose,” the court wrote.
 Much of the three-page decision addressed the Town’s compliance with the State Environmental Quality Review Act, known as SEQRA.
 The court rejected the club’s contention that the environmental review was improperly segmented—a practice in which related parts of a proposal are reviewed separately rather than considered together. It also upheld the Town’s classification of the acquisition as an “Unlisted” action under state environmental regulations.
 Even so, the judges noted that the Town had conducted the equivalent of the review associated with a Type I action, a classification that receives heightened environmental scrutiny.
 The court further rejected the argument that the Town completed its environmental review before obtaining the supporting evidence. When the Town issued its negative declaration—a finding that the proposal would not cause significant adverse environmental impacts requiring an environmental impact statement—it had all the information contained in the court record, the judges found.
 The Town had identified relevant environmental concerns, examined them sufficiently, and explained the basis for its determination; the court concluded.
 To Roxanne Fischer, a club member who has been vocal in her opposition to the acquisition, the Town’s decision has been fundamentally misguided. “This is far from the final word,” she said. (Photo by Tony Adamis) 
 The panel also upheld the Town Board’s handling of objections from the Waterfront Advisory Committee, which had found the proposal inconsistent with certain policies of the Town’s Local Waterfront Revitalization Plan.
 The Board considered each waterfront policy and provided written findings explaining why the acquisition was consistent with them, including the policies on which the advisory committee had reached a different conclusion, according to the decision.
 Wednesday’s ruling addresses a different governmental action from the zoning enactments struck down in earlier litigation.
 In June, Dutchess County Supreme Court Justice Maria Rosa annulled two local laws adopted in December 2025, along with their associated environmental determination. She found that the record submitted in that proceeding did not demonstrate an adequate assessment of the proposed park’s environmental effects. That ruling followed an earlier decision invalidating portions of a February 2025 zoning enactment.
 The appellate court’s new decision reviewed the July 2025 eminent domain determination directly. It does not expressly reverse those separate zoning rulings or reinstate the invalidated laws.
 The panel confirmed the acquisition determination, denied the club’s petition, and dismissed the proceeding on the merits, with costs.
 The decision does not address the amount the Town would pay for the property, a timetable for taking possession, or the effect of other litigation on the proposed acquisition.
 To Roxanne Fischer, a club member who has been vocal in her opposition to the acquisition, the Town’s decision has been fundamentally misguided. “Pushing ahead with eminent domain not only displaces a long-standing non-profit local institution, but it also commits Red Hook taxpayers to enormous legal expenses, acquisition costs, and significant future liabilities on a deeply problematic parcel,” she told The Daily Catch .
 Fischer said she expects the club’s legal team to continue seeking a way to prevent the acquisition, despite the court’s ruling. “This is far from the final word,” she said.
